cards.front: SGLT2 inhibitors beyond glucose lowering: main indications and key adverse effect?
cards.back: They block Na+-glucose reabsorption by SGLT2 in the proximal tubule. All reduce hospitalisation for heart failure; dapagliflozin reduced heart failure hospitalisation and cardiovascular death in HFrEF with or without diabetes. Canagliflozin, dapagliflozin and empagliflozin slowed progression of kidney disease in patients with reduced GFR and albuminuria. Adverse effects: genital mycotic infections (3-5% excess), urinary tract infections, volume depletion and hypotension; euglycaemic diabetic ketoacidosis has been reported.

cards.front: Finerenone: class, key use and key adverse effect?
cards.back: A non-steroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (FDA approved 2021) that competitively blocks aldosterone binding; it binds androgen and progesterone receptors less than spironolactone and distributes equally to heart and kidney. Use: CKD with type 2 diabetes, to reduce kidney function decline, non-fatal MI, heart failure hospitalisation and cardiovascular death. Key adverse effect: hyperkalaemia, less than with spironolactone or eplerenone but still significant. Metabolised by CYP3A4 (half-life about 2 h).

cards.front: Sacubitril-valsartan: what does each component do, and what is the key safety rule?
cards.back: Valsartan blocks AT1 receptors. Sacubitril is a prodrug whose active metabolite inhibits neprilysin, the enzyme that breaks down ANP and BNP (and also angiotensin II and bradykinin), so natriuretic peptide effects are enhanced. In HFrEF the combination was superior to enalapril, reducing cardiovascular death and hospitalisation. Because neprilysin also degrades bradykinin, angioedema is a concern, as with ACE inhibitors.

cards.front: Classify the mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists.
cards.text: Steroidal MRAs are {{spironolactone}} and {{eplerenone}}; the non-steroidal MRA is {{finerenone}}.

cards.front: Tirzepatide: mechanism, key use and key adverse effect?
cards.back: A dual GIP and GLP-1 receptor agonist: a modified GIP analogue given once weekly by subcutaneous injection. It raises glucose-dependent insulin release, lowers glucagon, slows gastric emptying and reduces appetite. In type 2 diabetes it lowered HbA1c by about 1.9-2.6% with weight loss of about 6-13 kg. Its safety profile is the same as the GLP-1 receptor agonists: mainly gastrointestinal effects, with the class caution against use in personal or family history of medullary thyroid cancer or MEN 2.

cards.front: Semaglutide: why is it used in obesity, and what is its key adverse effect?
cards.back: A long-acting, DPP-4-resistant GLP-1 receptor agonist given weekly by injection (an oral daily form also exists). Semaglutide 2.4 mg is approved for weight loss independent of diabetes status. Adverse effects of the class: nausea, vomiting, headache, anorexia and pancreatitis; C-cell tumours in rodents, so avoid with a history of medullary thyroid cancer or MEN 2.

cards.front: Inclisiran: how does it lower LDL-cholesterol, and how is it given?
cards.back: A small interfering RNA (FDA approved 2021) that targets PCSK9 mRNA in the liver and blocks PCSK9 synthesis. Fewer LDL receptors are degraded, so LDL-cholesterol falls by about 50%. Low-volume subcutaneous injections give effects lasting over 180 days, allowing twice-yearly dosing. Common adverse effects: injection-site reactions and bronchitis.

cards.front: Bempedoic acid: where does it act, and what adverse effects follow?
cards.back: An oral inhibitor of ATP-citrate lyase, acting in the liver in the cholesterol synthesis pathway at a step before HMG-CoA reductase; LDL receptors increase. Monotherapy lowers LDL-C by 15-25%; about 30% with ezetimibe (fixed combination available) and more with a statin. Adverse effects: hyperuricaemia (competition for renal OAT2) raising gout risk, tendon rupture, and rises in CK, creatinine and transaminases. Limit simvastatin to 20 mg and rosuvastatin to 40 mg when combined (myopathy).

cards.front: Classify the newer lipid-lowering drugs.
cards.text: Inclisiran is a {{small interfering RNA}} against {{PCSK9}} mRNA; bempedoic acid inhibits {{ATP-citrate lyase}}.

cards.front: Romosozumab: target, effect on bone, and key warning?
cards.back: A monoclonal antibody against sclerostin, an osteocyte protein that inhibits Wnt signalling and bone formation. Blocking it increases bone formation and also suppresses resorption. Given monthly by subcutaneous injection for one year, followed by an antiresorptive to keep the bone gained. Boxed warning: do not use in patients at risk of stroke or coronary vascular disease.

cards.front: Gepants: what are they, and which are used for acute treatment versus prevention of migraine?
cards.back: Small-molecule CGRP receptor antagonists. Trigeminal nerves release CGRP, an extremely powerful vasodilator, in migraine. First-generation gepants (olcegepant, telcagepant) worked but were limited by liver toxicity. Second generation: ubrogepant and rimegepant for acute attacks; rimegepant and atogepant for prevention.

cards.front: Classify the CGRP monoclonal antibodies used for migraine prevention.
cards.text: Erenumab binds the {{CGRP receptor}}, whereas eptinezumab, fremanezumab and galcanezumab bind the {{CGRP peptide}}; they are effective but injected and expensive, so they are {{second-line}} agents for migraine prevention.

cards.front: Aducanumab: target, use and main safety issue?
cards.back: A monoclonal antibody that reduces amyloid-beta plaques; the first disease-modifying therapy for Alzheimer disease (FDA 2021). Approval was via the Accelerated Approval Program on a surrogate (plaque burden) and was controversial, as clinical benefit was modest. Indication: mild cognitive impairment or mild dementia due to AD, with amyloid confirmed by PET or CSF. Given as monthly IV infusions. Main safety issue: amyloid-related imaging abnormalities (ARIA) in almost half of trial patients: cerebral oedema (ARIA-E) or microhaemorrhages (ARIA-H), often asymptomatic and reversible; MRI before starting and every 6 months. Donanemab is a newer anti-amyloid antibody.

cards.front: Classify the neurosteroid antidepressants.
cards.text: Brexanolone is a {{neurosteroid}} (allopregnanolone) that acts on {{GABA-A}} receptors; it is given as a {{60-hour}} IV infusion for postpartum depression.

cards.front: Bedaquiline: mechanism, use and key adverse effect?
cards.back: A diarylquinoline that inhibits mycobacterial ATP synthase, stopping energy production. Used in multidrug-resistant pulmonary TB as part of a combination. Metabolised by CYP3A4 to M2 (less active); terminal half-life about 5.5 months from tissue redistribution; strong CYP3A4 inhibitors or inducers interact. Adverse effects: nausea, arthralgia, headache; hepatotoxicity; boxed warning for QTc prolongation and associated mortality.

cards.front: Pretomanid: how is it activated, what is its spectrum, and what is a key interaction?
cards.back: A nitroimidazole prodrug activated inside M. tuberculosis by a deazaflavin (F420)-dependent nitroreductase. In replicating bacilli it blocks mycolic acid synthesis; in non-replicating anaerobic bacilli it releases nitric oxide. Active against M. tuberculosis only, not other mycobacteria. Used with bedaquiline and linezolid for 6 months in XDR, pre-XDR or non-responsive MDR pulmonary TB. Partly metabolised by CYP3A4, so avoid potent CYP3A4 inducers (rifampicin lowers its levels). Can raise liver enzymes.

cards.front: Cefiderocol: how does it enter bacteria, and when is it reserved?
cards.back: A siderophore cephalosporin. Unlike other beta-lactams, which diffuse through porins, it is bound by bacterial active iron transporters and pumped into the cell, then binds PBPs to inhibit cell wall synthesis. It is stable to all beta-lactamase types, including metallo-beta-lactamases, and is active against drug-resistant Enterobacterales (including carbapenem-resistant), Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Acinetobacter baumannii, but not Gram-positives or anaerobes. Warning: increased mortality in carbapenem-resistant infections in one trial, so reserve it for cases with limited or no alternatives.

cards.front: Baloxavir marboxil: target, dosing principle and key adverse effect?
cards.back: An oral prodrug hydrolysed to baloxavir acid, which inhibits the influenza cap-dependent endonuclease, blocking initiation of viral mRNA synthesis. Active against influenza A and B, including oseltamivir-resistant virus. Single-dose treatment of uncomplicated influenza within 2 days of symptoms in patients 12 years and older, and post-exposure prophylaxis. Long half-life (about 80 h). Avoid co-administration with dairy products or polyvalent cations. Resistance: polymerase acidic protein I38T/M/F variants emerged in about 10% of treated patients.

cards.front: Classify the oral COVID-19 antiviral nirmatrelvir.
cards.text: Nirmatrelvir inhibits the viral {{main protease (MPRO)}}; it is given with low-dose {{ritonavir}}, a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor that raises and prolongs its levels, causing many {{CYP3A}} drug interactions.

cards.front: Molnupiravir: mechanism and key restriction?
cards.back: An oral prodrug of the ribonucleoside beta-D-N4-hydroxycytidine (NHC). Its triphosphate is taken up by the viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, causing mutations and lethal mutagenesis. Used within 5 days of symptoms in non-hospitalised mild to moderate COVID-19 at high risk of progression, under Emergency Use Authorization; less effective than nirmatrelvir-ritonavir. Contraindicated in pregnancy and lactation (developmental toxicity in animals) and not used under 18 years (bone and cartilage).

cards.front: CTLA-4 and PD-1 checkpoint inhibitors: where do they act, and which agents block each?
cards.back: CTLA-4 competes with CD28 for B7 ligands on antigen-presenting cells, damping T-cell priming. Anti-CTLA-4 antibodies (ipilimumab, tremelimumab) release this brake early, in lymphoid tissue. PD-1 on activated T cells binds PD-L1 and PD-L2, exhausting T cells within tumours. Anti-PD-1 (nivolumab, pembrolizumab, cemiplimab) and anti-PD-L1 (atezolizumab, durvalumab, avelumab) restore antitumour activity.

Liver: immune-mediated hepatitis

Lung: pneumonitis; also nephritis

Anti-PD-1 agents: immune-mediated reactions much less common
Withhold for moderate reactions until baseline
High-dose corticosteroids for severe reactions
Discontinue for severe pneumonitis, colitis, hepatitis or nephritis

cards.front: Sotorasib: which mutation does it target, how does it bind, and what are its key adverse effects?
cards.back: A first-in-class oral covalent inhibitor of KRAS G12C, approved in 2021. It bonds irreversibly to the cysteine present only in the mutant protein, locking KRAS in the inactive (GDP-bound) state and blocking downstream signalling. Used in locally advanced or metastatic NSCLC with KRAS G12C after at least one prior systemic therapy (about 13% of NSCLC carry it). Adverse effects: diarrhoea, nausea, low-grade hepatotoxicity; rarely pneumonitis and dyspnoea. Metabolised partly by CYP3A.
